required_fixes: Add disclosure of how Board/committee responsibilities for climate- and sustainability-related risks and opportunities are reflected in formal governance documents (terms of reference/mandates/role descriptions/related policies).

Explain the process used by the Board to determine whether appropriate climate/sustainability skills and competencies are available or will be developed (eg, skills matrix, periodic assessment, training plan governance).

Expand on how the Board takes climate/sustainability matters into account in (i) strategy oversight, (ii) major transactions (describe the 'climate check' at least at a procedural level), and (iii) risk management processes/related policies, including whether/how trade-offs are considered.

For targets: describe how the Board oversees target-setting and progress monitoring (what targets/metrics, cadence, dashboards/committees), and clarify how performance metrics are incorporated into remuneration policies (not only the 8.7% figure).
For management’s role: describe how oversight is exercised over the Group Sustainability Committee (reporting lines, approvals/escalation, interaction with Board/ESG committee).

Describe management controls/procedures used to monitor/manage/oversee climate/sustainability risks and opportunities and how these integrate with other internal functions (eg, risk, finance, internal audit, compliance).
ifrs_coverage_judge.summary: The draft provides several governance facts (Board identification, meeting cadence, semi-annual climate reporting, committee existence, skills programme, ERM integration statement, major transaction climate check, and remuneration linkage). However, multiple mandatory IFRS S1/S2 governance requirements are not fully met because the section lacks required process-level disclosures: linkage to formal mandates/terms of reference, how skills needs are determined, how the Board considers climate/sustainability in strategy/transactions/risk management including trade-offs, how targets are set/monitored and embedded in remuneration policy, and how management oversight/controls are exercised and integrated across internal functions. No invented 'missing data' language was found.

unsupported_claims.claim_text: During the period, the Board met in full session four times per year.
unsupported_claims.why_unsupported: Evidence shows conflicting board meeting frequencies (4 in governance[0], but 7 in governance[1] and 8 in governance[2]) and the draft does not specify which period/index applies.

unsupported_claims.claim_text: Board oversight is supported by climate-related competence within the Board. 33.5% of directors are assessed as having climate expertise.
unsupported_claims.why_unsupported: Evidence contains multiple different values (33.5, 35.5, 37.5) and the draft does not specify which period/index applies; reporting_kpis shows 37.5, not 33.5.

unsupported_claims.claim_text: An ESG committee operates as part of the governance structure. During the period, the ESG committee met five times per year.
unsupported_claims.why_unsupported: Evidence contains multiple different values (5, 6, 7) and the draft does not specify which period/index applies; reporting_kpis shows 7, not 5.

unsupported_claims.claim_text: During the period, the named management committee was the Group Sustainability Committee.
unsupported_claims.why_unsupported: Evidence shows different management committee names across governance indices; the draft does not specify which period/index applies.

unsupported_claims.claim_text: Across the executive population, 8.7% of executive remuneration is linked to climate-related measures.
unsupported_claims.why_unsupported: Evidence contains multiple different values (8.7, 15.3, 15.1) and the draft does not specify which period/index applies.

questionable_claims.claim_text: Oversight is managed on an integrated basis and is therefore described in a single, integrated governance disclosure.
questionable_claims.why_questionable: No direct evidence item demonstrates 'integrated' oversight (e.g., terms of reference, governance model, role descriptions). Existing evidence supports some governance metrics but not the integration assertion.

questionable_claims.claim_text: The Board is the primary governance body overseeing climate-related and sustainability-related risks and opportunities.
questionable_claims.why_questionable: No direct evidence (e.g., board charter/mandate) is provided to substantiate primacy of Board oversight versus committees/management; evidence only shows meeting/reporting metrics.

questionable_claims.claim_text: Climate-related matters were integrated into Board deliberations and decision-making.
questionable_claims.why_questionable: Board minutes show climate topics discussed, but 'integrated into decision-making' implies a process/impact not evidenced beyond topic presence.

questionable_claims.claim_text: The Group Sustainability Committee supports management oversight ... and provides inputs for escalation ... including the semi-annual climate risk reporting to the Board.
questionable_claims.why_questionable: Evidence supports existence of a management committee name (in one index) and semi-annual reporting, but not the described escalation mechanics or that this specific committee is the source of the Board reporting.

questionable_claims.claim_text: Climate-related and sustainability-related risks and opportunities are integrated into the organisation’s enterprise risk management processes.
questionable_claims.why_questionable: Evidence includes a boolean flag (erm_integration_flag=True) but no description of how integration occurs; still minimally supported as a high-level statement.

questionable_claims.claim_text: Climate-related considerations are incorporated into decision-making on major transactions through a climate check for major transactions.
questionable_claims.why_questionable: Evidence includes a boolean flag (major_transactions_climate_check=True) but no detail on scope/criteria/ownership; statement is directionally supported but underspecified.

required_fixes: Specify the reporting period and align all quantitative values to the correct dataset slice (e.g., governance[0] vs governance[1] vs governance[2]) or update the narrative to match the selected period’s evidence.

Resolve conflicts between narrative/Table 1 and evidence for: Board meeting frequency, Board climate expertise %, ESG committee meeting frequency, management committee name, and % of executive remuneration linked to climate measures.

If claiming 'integrated oversight' and 'Board is primary governance body', add supporting evidence references (e.g., board/committee terms of reference, governance charter) or soften/rephrase to what is evidenced (e.g., 'Board receives semi-annual climate risk reporting and discusses climate topics').

For the management committee and escalation flow, either (a) provide evidence that the named committee produces/escalates the semi-annual Board reporting, or (b) reword to a generic statement supported by evidence (committee exists; Board receives semi-annual reporting).
Keep Table 1 consistent with the corrected narrative values and the chosen evidence source.
evidence_judge.summary: The section contains several materially unsupported quantitative claims due to conflicting evidence across governance indices (meeting frequency, expertise %, committee meetings, management committee name, remuneration linkage). Several qualitative statements (integrated oversight, primary governance body, decision-making integration, escalation flow) are also undersupported because the provided evidence does not include mandates/charters or process documentation. Correct by selecting the correct period/index, aligning numbers, and adding governance mandate/process evidence or softening claims.

voice_issues: Voice is generally neutral and formal, but it does not consistently use standards-oriented verbs (e.g., 'oversees', 'reviews', 'monitors') even though the content would support them.
The section uses third-person consistently, which is acceptable, but it does not explicitly distinguish externally defined requirements from entity actions (minor issue).
structure_issues: The section does not open with a high-level framing paragraph linking governance of sustainability/climate to the business model and operations, as required by the section_style.
Subsections generally lack explicit one-sentence purpose statements before details (e.g., 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, etc.).
Most subsections do not close with a short connectivity sentence linking to related sections or financial statements.
The structure is largely narrative; it does not use role blocks or a governance body/role-to-responsibility mapping table, which is preferred for scanability and evidence.
The section references only one table and no figures; the style guide prefers a governance structure figure and more explicit use of tables for role/responsibility mapping.
Principles/what vs mechanics/how are not clearly separated with subheadings; many subsections mix mandate and mechanics in the same short paragraph.
wording_issues: Some sentences are descriptive but could be more aligned with preferred governance verbs (e.g., 'is the primary governance body' could be 'oversees', 'monitors', 'reviews').

A few phrases are slightly interpretive rather than strictly evidence-led (e.g., 'These agenda items indicate that Board oversight covered both review of climate-related strategic responses...' reads as commentary rather than pure process evidence).

The section does not explicitly distinguish between current-period facts, estimates/judgements, and forward-looking intentions; all content is presented as factual without clarifying where assessments (e.g., 'assessed as having climate expertise') involve judgement.
Percentages and meeting frequencies are used even though the section_style explicitly discourages numeric values such as meeting frequencies and KPI weights in template text.
table_figure_issues: Table 1 has a clear title and number, but the caption is somewhat generic and does not describe purpose beyond 'Selected governance indicators'; the style guide prefers more descriptive captions.
The narrative introduces Table 1, but it does not return to interpret or contextualise the indicators after the table.
The table uses mostly single-word or very short entries rather than short narrative snippets that describe the indicator, which is preferred in the style guide.
No governance structure figure is provided, despite the figure_usage guidance that strongly prefers a governance structure diagram for this section.
required_fixes: Add an opening framing paragraph for Section 1 that links governance of sustainability- and climate-related matters to the business model, strategy, and operations, and clarifies that the section explains oversight, decision rights, and integration with enterprise risk management.

For each subsection (1.1–1.9), add a one-sentence purpose statement at the start that explains what the subsection covers and why it matters for governance (e.g., 'This subsection describes how the Board oversees climate-related and sustainability-related risks and opportunities.').

Introduce short connectivity sentences at the end of major subsections (e.g., 1.1, 1.5, 1.6, 1.8) that link to related sections such as Strategy, Risk Management, and Metrics and Targets using generic cross-reference placeholders (e.g., 'Refer to [Section: Strategy] for how these governance arrangements inform transition planning.').

Recast key sentences to use preferred governance verbs and IFRS-style language (e.g., 'The Board oversees...', 'The ESG committee reviews and recommends...', 'The Group Sustainability Committee monitors and escalates...') while keeping the neutral, non-promotional tone.

Clarify where statements involve judgement or assessment, such as the percentage of directors with climate expertise, by briefly indicating that this is based on an internal skills assessment or defined criteria, without adding personal data.

Remove or generalise specific numeric values that the section_style flags as not suitable for reusable templates (e.g., exact Board size, meeting frequencies, percentages of agenda items and remuneration linkage). Replace them with qualitative descriptors (e.g., 'a majority of', 'a portion of', 'on a regular basis') or, if numbers must be retained for this target report, ensure they are clearly presented as current-period facts and not embedded in template language.

Enhance Table 1 to align with the preferred evidence style: expand cells into short narrative snippets that describe each indicator (definition, scope, and cadence) rather than only listing a value; ensure the caption explains that the table provides a summary of key governance indicators for climate- and sustainability-related oversight.

After Table 1, add a brief narrative paragraph that interprets the table at a high level (e.g., what the indicators collectively show about governance cadence and coverage) without becoming promotional.

Consider adding an additional table that maps governance bodies (Board, ESG committee, Group Sustainability Committee, management) to their responsibilities, decision rights, and reporting lines for climate- and sustainability-related matters, in line with the table_usage guidance.

Add a reference to a governance structure figure (even if the figure itself is developed at layout stage), with a caption that explains the information flow and accountability relationships; ensure the narrative briefly explains what the figure shows.

Ensure that all content remains neutral and evidence-led; remove or soften interpretive phrases such as 'These agenda items indicate that...' and instead describe the scope of oversight directly (e.g., 'Board oversight covers review of strategic responses and monitoring of progress and incentives.').

Confirm that no missing data exists for required governance disclosures; if any governance information is not available or not applicable, explicitly state this using the missing_data_language_rules (what is missing, why, interim approach, limitations, and planned enhancement).
style_judge.summary: The section is broadly aligned with the formal, neutral, IFRS-style governance disclosure voice and uses clear headings, bullets, and a numbered table. However, it does not fully follow the approved authoring style in terms of layered structure, explicit purpose and connectivity sentences, preferred governance verbs, and evidence presentation. Numeric details such as meeting frequencies and KPI weights conflict with the section_style guidance for reusable templates. Table 1 is present but could be more descriptive and better integrated into the narrative, and the section lacks the preferred governance structure figure and role-to-responsibility mapping. With targeted revisions to structure, wording, and table usage, the section can be brought to an approval standard, but in its current form it should be revised rather than approved.
